summary: This note, drawn from a Wikipedia article on the Dominican Order, covers English Dominican mysticism, which centred on the moral imitation of Christ and a structured love of fellow men rather than ecstatic union. It then traces the order's intellectual and spiritual history through Humbert of Romans, who emphasized preaching and linguistic study, and Albertus Magnus, who shaped Dominican education and introduced Aristotle. It closes with the moral view of humanity as the image of God.
one_line: Overview of the Dominican Order's late medieval English mysticism, its preaching and scholarship under Humbert of Romans and Albertus Magnus, and its view of humanity as God's image.
key_facts: English Dominican mysticism's ultimate focus was on a crucial dynamic in one's personal relationship with God, namely moral imitation of the Savior.

Four elements characterized English Dominican mysticism: spiritual emulation of the moral essence of Christ's life, a link between that emulation and humanity's disposition as images of the divine, an embodied spirituality with structured love of fellow men at its center, and an aspiration toward ethical or actual union with God.
Humbert of Romans was master general of the order from 1254 to 1263.
Humbert of Romans's tenure as master general was when the sisters in the order were given official membership.
Humbert of Romans encouraged linguistic studies among the Dominicans, primarily Arabic, for missionary work in the Middle East.
Humbert of Romans regarded excellence in preaching as his most lasting contribution to the order.
Albertus Magnus was the only person of the period to be given the appellation "Great".
Albertus Magnus was a scientist, philosopher, astrologer, theologian, spiritual writer, ecumenist, and diplomat.
Under Humbert of Romans, Albert molded the curriculum of studies for all Dominican students and introduced Aristotle to the classroom.
The thirty years of work by Thomas Aquinas and Albert (1245–1274) allowed Aristotelian study to be included in the curriculum of Dominican schools.
Albert's study of Dionysus the Areopagite was one of his greatest contributions.

A movement associated with Meister Eckhart, Heinrich Suso, Johannes Tauler, and St. Catherine of Siena arose especially in Germany and Italy, and was the prelude to reforms undertaken by Raymond of Capua at the end of the century.
The mystical movement assumed remarkable proportions in the congregations of Lombardy and the Netherlands, and in the reforms of Savonarola in Florence.
English Dominican spirituality concentrated on the moral implications of image-bearing rather than the philosophical foundations of the imago Dei.
